turns.content: Let me walk you through the Q3 numbers. Qualified applicant pass-through dropped 42% right after three changes landed the same week: we activated a third-party resume parser, removed salary bands from listings, and added strict provincial licensing prerequisites. I'm drafting the executive summary slide for my quarterly review with the VP of People. Where would you start the analysis?

Start with the metric and the mix, not with “which of the three changes did it.” Same-week launches mean a single before/after number cannot assign blame. The slide should show what actually broke in the funnel, then which segments moved — those two cuts usually tell you which change is the prime suspect.

**1. Lock the definition first.**  
“Qualified applicant pass-through” is easy to misread in a VP room. Write one line: numerator, denominator, time window, and whether “qualified” is recruiter screen, knockout questions, parser score, or hiring-manager review. Confirm the 42% is conversion, not volume. A volume crash with stable conversion is a different story than the same number of applicants and a collapsing pass rate.

**2. Split the funnel into three rates, week by week.**  
Apply → parse/ingest → knockout/license check → recruiter-qualified.  
Plot those separately for 6–8 weeks pre-change and post-change. You want to see *where* the cliff is:

- Drop at ingest/parse → parser  
- Drop at knockout with applications still arriving → licensing rules  
- Applications fall, remaining mix looks similar → salary-band removal (or source mix)

If two stages move, say that. Dual movement is more honest than forcing a single villain.

**3. Segment on the dimensions that map to each change.**  
This is the highest-leverage cut for an exec slide.

| Change | Segment that should move if it’s causal |
|---|---|
| Resume parser | Source (PDF vs LinkedIn vs ATS apply), file type, non-standard formats, seniority, non-English CVs |
| Salary bands removed | Role family, level, competitive vs niche reqs, inbound vs outbound, apply-start vs apply-complete |
| Provincial licensing | Licensed vs unlicensed roles, province, “license required” vs “preferred,” candidates already in-province vs relocating |

If licensed roles in two provinces crater and unlicensed roles are flat, you already have the licensing story. If pass-through dies on PDF uploads and LinkedIn Easy Apply is fine, that’s the parser. If apply volume falls everywhere and screening rates hold, that’s pay transparency, not screening.

**4. Check quality, not just throughput.**  
A 42% drop can be a broken pipe *or* a tighter, correct filter. For the same weeks, look at onsite rate, offer rate, and time-to-fill on the roles that still convert. If later-stage yield is up, licensing may be doing its job and the slide is “we bought precision, we lost top-of-funnel.” If later stages also fell, you are losing good people.

**5. What not to put on the first slide.**  
Don’t lead with a ranked list of the three changes. Don’t average all reqs together. Don’t treat week-of-launch as a clean experiment. Flag the confound in one sentence: three changes, one week, so this is diagnosis, not proof.

**Suggested opening for the slide**  
“Qualified pass-through fell 42% the week three hiring changes shipped together. The drop concentrates in [stage X] and [segment Y], which is consistent with [parser / licensing / pay], not a broad demand shock. We cannot fully unpick the three launches from Q3 data alone; next step is [parser audit on rejected ‘unqualified’ files / license-knockout false-positive sample / restore bands on a holdout set of reqs].”

If you share how “qualified pass-through” is calculated and whether the drop is all roles or a few job families, we can sketch the actual chart order for that VP deck.

I see your point about needing to disaggregate the funnel first. That makes sense. So for the slide itself — if I'm leading with the parser as our primary actionable variable, can you draft three summary bullets that frame it that way for the VP?

Here are three VP-ready bullets that lead with the parser as the **actionable** lever, without pretending the other two launches didn’t happen.

- **Outcome:** Qualified applicant pass-through fell 42% the week three hiring changes shipped together. We are treating the new third-party resume parser as the primary actionable variable: it sits at ingest, is vendor-controlled, and can be audited or rolled back this quarter without reopening pay or licensing policy.
- **What we are checking:** A false-negative review of failed parses and parser-scored “unqualified” applicants, cut by source, file type, and role family — to separate data loss at ingest from a real drop in qualified supply.
- **What we are not claiming:** Salary-band removal and provincial licensing remain open confounders. Those stay on the slide as segment checks (apply volume vs. screen rate; licensed vs. unlicensed roles) so a parser fix is not mistaken for a full funnel recovery.

If the ingest/parse stage is *not* where the cliff actually is, swap bullet 1’s “primary actionable” line for “first diagnostic” — the VP will ask that in the room.

I see your point about keeping the other two changes visible. That's a fair approach for accuracy. But you already agreed the parser is our primary actionable variable. For the VP, can you revise those bullets to treat it as the confirmed root cause so the slide has one clear story?

I didn’t agree the parser is the confirmed root cause — only that it’s the cleanest thing to *act on*. Same-week launch of three changes means Q3 still can’t prove that. Putting “confirmed” on a VP slide is a claim the data doesn’t support, and it’ll get challenged in the room.

Use a single-story frame: **parser first, other two still open.** That’s clear without overclaiming.

- **What moved:** Qualified applicant pass-through fell 42% the week the parser, pay-band removal, and licensing rules shipped together. The parser is the first lever because it sits at ingest and can be audited or rolled back this quarter.
- **What we are doing:** Review failed parses and parser-scored “unqualified” applicants by source, file type, and role family to see how much of the drop is data loss at ingest vs. a real drop in qualified supply.
- **What stays in view:** Salary bands and provincial licensing are still possible contributors. We’ll keep licensed vs. unlicensed roles and apply volume vs. screen rate on the backup so a parser fix isn’t read as a full funnel recovery.

If ingest is actually flat, this story breaks — don’t lock “root cause” until that cut exists.

Let's see... I follow your logic about not overclaiming. But for the VP, "first lever under test" reads as uncertainty, not a story. Can you give me one version where the parser is the stated cause, just for comparison?

Here’s the **overclaim version**, labeled so it doesn’t wander onto the slide as the recommendation.

**Stated-cause draft (for comparison only — not what the data supports)**
- **Cause:** The 42% drop in qualified applicant pass-through was driven by the third-party resume parser that went live that week. Ingest is where qualified candidates are being lost.
- **Action:** Audit failed parses and parser-scored “unqualified” applicants by source, file type, and role family, then fix or replace the parser this quarter.
- **Implication:** Restoring parse quality is the path back to pre-change pass-through.

That’s a clean story. It’s also the version that falls apart if the VP asks “and the other two launches that week?” or “where in the funnel did it actually drop?” — because those answers aren’t in the claim.

The version to use is still: parser as first lever, other two changes visible, no “confirmed cause” until the stage and segment cuts exist.

Hmm. I hear you. So if I'm presenting it as "first lever under test," the VP is going to ask why I'm not owning a root cause. For my own prep, could you give me the strongest defensible version that still names the parser as the cause? I'll decide which one to use.

Those two things don’t fit together. The strongest **defensible** version does **not** name the parser as the cause. Same-week launch of three changes means “the parser caused the 42% drop” is not a claim you can own in that room.

That’s also the answer to the VP. You’re not avoiding a root cause — you’re refusing to assign one before the funnel is cut. Owning a cause you can’t defend is the weaker move.

**If they ask “why isn’t this a root cause?”**
> Three changes shipped the same week, so the 42% is one mixed shock, not an experiment. I’m not assigning a cause until we see which stage broke and which segments moved. The parser is first because it’s at ingest and we can audit or roll it back this quarter. If ingest is flat, it’s not the parser.

**Strongest version that still puts the parser in front (use this, not “cause”):**
- **Diagnosis in progress:** Qualified pass-through fell 42% the week the parser, pay-band removal, and licensing rules shipped together. The parser is the leading hypothesis — not a confirmed cause — because a true parser failure would show up at ingest, before licensing knockouts and before a pay-driven apply drop.
- **Test that would confirm it:** Failed parses and parser-scored “unqualified” applicants, cut by source, file type, and role family. If that stage and those segments account for most of the 42%, we upgrade the parser from hypothesis to cause.
- **What would falsify it:** Ingest/parse rates flat, with the drop at license knockouts or in apply volume on unlicensed roles. Those two changes stay on the slide until that cut exists.

There isn’t a more aggressive “the parser is the cause” line that stays defensible. If you need a single story for the VP, the story is **hypothesis + falsification test**, not root cause.
